intro_questions.title: Knowledge Questions
intro_questions.description: These questions test your knowledge of MLOps and ML related concepts and principles. We will ask you to answer the same questions again when you have completed the serious game session to measure your learning progress.
intro_questions.question: What is 'concept drift' in the context of Machine Learning?

answers.text: **Model accuracy declines over time** as real-world data gradually shifts or trends change.
The model's **code becomes incompatible** with updated software libraries over time.
**Intentionally shifting parameters** during training to prevent vanishing gradients.
A **security attack** that plants subtle biases in training data to trigger specific failures.

intro_questions.question: What is the difference between Machine Learning (ML) and Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) ?

answers.text: ML covers **model creation and evaluation**; MLOps covers **deployment, monitoring, and production maintenance**.
ML is **theoretical algorithm design**; MLOps is only **empirical testing and tuning**.
ML handles **data exploration and training**; MLOps is a **one-time handoff** to operations.
ML **maximizes accuracy** on isolated datasets; MLOps focuses on **feature engineering and data augmentation**.

intro_questions.question: What does the MLOps principle of 'Reproducibility' ensure?

answers.text: An experiment gives **identical results** when repeated with the same data and environment.
**Tracing a prediction back** to the exact data and code version that produced it.
**Automatically re-running training** whenever input data shifts significantly.
**Consistent performance metrics** across multiple validation datasets.

intro_questions.question: What impacts could unmanaged pipeline complexity (pipeline jungles) have?

answers.text: **Hard to trace which data version** trained a deployed model, making results difficult to reproduce or debug.
**Hyperparameter search grows harder** with each added pipeline, degrading performance.
**Deployment slows down** as each new step needs approval before serving.
**Monitoring gets harder** as alerts spread across many pipelines, delaying fixes.

intro_questions.title: Stakeholder Perspective
intro_questions.description: These questions describe how someone in a project might act or think, without naming their job. Pick which role fits best.
intro_questions.question: When last Tuesday's numbers don't line up with the week before, they want to know exactly why the input changed, not just whether the results at the end still look reasonable.
When someone proposes a new project, they want to know which number on the weekly report would actually move, and by how much, before agreeing to spend a cent on it.
After watching three different teams each hit the same manual release snag in the same week, they're the one who builds a single tool so none of them have to do it by hand again.
Before anyone signs off on using this data, they want to know exactly what the agreement with the customer actually permits, not just what the system is technically capable of.
Even with the same input, they'll keep comparing new candidate approaches against each other, unwilling to settle until one clearly beats the rest.
Once a candidate approach is chosen, they're the one who wires it up so the rest of the system can call it on its own, not just watch someone trigger it manually.
When a plan satisfies every rule on paper, they're still the one who can tell you it won't survive contact with how people actually do this job day to day.

intro_questions.title: Trade-off Scenarios
intro_questions.description: These describe a disagreement between two roles on a project similar to yours. Pick the best answer for each.
intro_questions.question: A regional distributor needs a restocking model shipped before a two-day cold-chain audit deadline. The ML engineer wants to deploy now with a manual sign-off instead of the full data-protection review. The legal expert insists every release passes that review first, even if it slips the deadline. Which resolution best matches how such trade-offs are usually handled?

answers.text: They agree on an **interim check** now, with the **fuller review** following shortly after.
They complete the **full review** first, and the **deadline** moves instead.
They proceed **without telling** the other side.
Someone **outside the disagreement** makes the call instead.

intro_questions.question: A cold snap threatens frozen-goods demand forecasts. The business stakeholder needs a stock decision within the hour. The data engineer wants to pause integrating a new weather feed into the pipeline until it's validated, worried a rushed integration corrupts the pipeline. Which of these is the most accurate description of the data engineer's real objection?

answers.text: Integrating an **unvalidated feed** risks **corrupting the pipeline** for everyone, not just this one decision.
The new feed comes from a **vendor** the data engineer personally **distrusts**.
**Automating** the integration would take too much **engineering time** this week.
The business stakeholder's **timeline** doesn't match the usual **release schedule**.

intro_questions.question: A demand-forecasting model flags a sudden drop for one product category. The subject matter expert says the drop is expected, a known seasonal pattern the model wasn't around to learn yet. The ML engineer wants to retrain immediately on the new numbers before anyone acts on the forecast. Which resolution best fits how this kind of disagreement usually gets resolved?

answers.text: They fold the **seasonal pattern** into the forecast before **retraining** on anything else.
They **retrain** on the newest numbers and treat the seasonal explanation as **unconfirmed**.
They **leave the forecast as it is**, since revisiting it would cost more time than it's worth.
They put the decision in front of whoever manages the model's **overall roadmap**.
